sc-compare-equal.prompt: Which expression checks whether `score` is equal to `10`?

help.concept: `==` compares values, while `=` assigns a value.

sc-truthy-string.prompt: What value does the expression `4 <= 4` produce?
sc-truthy-string.hint: The operator includes equality as well as less-than.

help.concept: `<=` is true when the left value is less than or equal to the right value.
help.hint_1: Here the two numbers are equal.
help.hint_2: Comparison expressions produce the boolean values `True` or `False`.

mc-true-comparisons.title: Choose all true comparisons
mc-true-comparisons.prompt: Which expressions evaluate to `True`? Choose all that apply.
mc-true-comparisons.hint: Evaluate each relationship exactly as written.

help.hint_1: `6 >= 6` is true because equality is allowed.
help.hint_2: `3 != 5` is true because the values differ.

mc-falsey-values.title: Choose the false comparison results
mc-falsey-values.prompt: Which expressions evaluate to `False`? Choose all that apply.
mc-falsey-values.hint: Evaluate each comparison one at a time.

help.concept: A comparison is false when the relationship written by its operator does not hold.
help.hint_2: Do not confuse the string `"False"` with the boolean value `False`.

compare-operators.title: Compare values with Python operators
compare-operators.bodyMarkdown:
Comparison operators ask whether two values have a particular relationship.

Every comparison expression evaluates to exactly one boolean value: `True` or `False`.

Common comparison operators are:

- `==` — equal to
- `!=` — not equal to
- `>` — greater than
- `<` — less than
- `>=` — greater than or equal to
- `<=` — less than or equal to

```python
print(5 > 3)
print(5 == 3)
print(7 != 7)
```

Output:

```text
True
False
False
```

`=` and `==` have different jobs:

```python
score = 10      # assignment
score == 10     # comparison
```

Use `=` to store a value. Use `==` to ask whether two values are equal.

truth-values-in-conditions.title: Store and print comparison results
truth-values-in-conditions.bodyMarkdown:
A comparison is an expression, so its boolean result can be stored in a variable.

```python
age = 16
old_enough = age >= 13

print(old_enough)
```

Output:

```text
True
```

You can read that flow in two steps:

1. `age >= 13` is evaluated;
2. the resulting boolean is stored in `old_enough`.

The variable does not store the comparison text. It stores the result: either `True` or `False`.

Another example:

```python
score = 72
passed = score >= 70

print(passed)
```

Output:

```text
True
```

Later lessons will use these boolean results to control which blocks run. For now, focus on creating and inspecting the comparison result itself.

truthiness-basics.title: Compare input values without branching
truthiness-basics.bodyMarkdown:
Comparisons also work with values read from input.

For numeric comparisons, convert the input text first:

```python
age = int(input())
print(age >= 18)
```

If the input is `20`, the output is:

```text
True
```

If the input is `14`, the output is:

```text
False
```

You can compare two input values too:

```python
first = int(input())
second = int(input())

print(first == second)
print(first != second)
```

For equal inputs, the first line is `True` and the second is `False`.

This lesson stops at producing boolean results. The next conditional lessons will decide what code to run based on those results.
